analysis.one_liner: Shields lenders from new mortgage-lending data rules and blocks public release of expanded loan data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee after a January 2018 subcommittee hearing, so the expanded mortgage-disclosure rules stayed in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2015, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau expanded a decades-old law that requires banks to report detailed data on their home mortgage lending — data the public can use to see whether lenders are serving or shunning particular neighborhoods. This bill would have barred regulators from penalizing banks that failed to comply with the expanded reporting rules before 2019 or 2020, and would have permanently barred the government from releasing any of the new loan-level data fields to the public, leaving only old aggregate summaries available [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Depository institutions — banks and credit unions that make home mortgages — would save the cost of collecting, reporting, and facing enforcement over the expanded loan-level data. They would also be shielded from lawsuits tied to the new requirements [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and credit unions making mortgages

how_it_helps.text: Blocks supervisory, enforcement, and private suits against depository institutions for noncompliance with the expanded data-collection rule (section 1003.4) before January 1, 2019, and the expanded reporting rule (section 1003.5) before January 1, 2020 [S3].

Prohibits banks and the CFPB from publishing or disclosing any HMDA data fields not required before the Dodd-Frank Act, beyond old-style aggregate statistics — permanently removing the new loan-level details from public view [S3].
Relieves lenders of the cost of collecting and reporting the additional data points added by the CFPB's 2015 and 2017 rules, which the bill's sponsor framed as regulatory relief [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Homebuyers, renters, and community organizations that rely on Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data to identify neighborhoods being underserved by lenders, and fair-lending regulators who use the loan-level detail to detect discrimination and redlining. The bill would strip the newest, most revealing data from public view while leaving existing rules otherwise in place [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The expanded HMDA data is the primary public tool for detecting discriminatory or redlined mortgage lending; removing it from public release would leave community groups and regulators with only coarse aggregate statistics [S2, S3].

A good-faith objection from lenders is real: collecting dozens of new data points per loan imposes compliance costs, particularly on smaller institutions, and a compliance deadline shield is a narrower remedy than the permanent data blackout this bill also contains [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance-relief half of the bill addresses a genuine gripe about regulatory burden, but the bill goes well beyond a delay: it permanently withholds the new loan-level data from the public, weakening the main transparency tool that has existed since 1975 for seeing where banks do and do not lend. The costs to fair-lending oversight outweigh the compliance savings, and the bill never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested in a debate or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced; the committee held one subcommittee hearing on it in January 2018, but never voted it out, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Representative Tom Emmer introduced the bill on December 14, 2017, with Representative Randy Hultgren as its sole cosponsor [S1, S4].
It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the same day [S5].
The Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit held a hearing on the bill on January 9, 2018 — the last action it received [S5].
The committee never reported the bill to the House floor and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage borrowers, community groups, and fair-lending enforcers, who keep full public access to loan-level mortgage data; banks do not get the exemption they sought.

for.name: Rep. Tom Emmer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 14, 2017 to delay and scale back the CFPB's expanded home-mortgage data rules.

for.name: Rep. Randy Hultgren
for.role: Sole cosponsor; chaired the Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, and his subcommittee held a hearing on it on January 9, 2018.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jeb Hensarling, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee for a hearing but never took a markup vote or reported it to the House floor, letting it die.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. Both the sponsor and the only cosponsor were Republicans, and the bill died in committee of the Republican-controlled House without floor consideration [S1, S4, S5].

industries.industry: Depository institutions (banks and credit unions making home mortgages)
industries.note: The bill would exempt them from penalties for skipping the expanded mortgage-data reporting and permanently block public release of the new loan-level data, saving compliance costs. The public relies on that same data to spot underserved neighborhoods, so the banks' gain is the public's loss of transparency.

industries.industry: Consumer and community advocacy groups using HMDA data
industries.note: These groups use loan-level mortgage data to document redlining and press lenders to serve all communities; the bill would cut off the new detailed data from public release.
